title: Neurophos Raises $110 Million for Optical Chips: Claims Compute Power at Same Power Consumption is 25x That of GPUs
source_used: TechFlow (full text); funding date checked on SiliconANGLE, 22 Jan 2026
key_facts: Neurophos, based in Austin, Texas, builds an optical computing unit (OCU) that does AI calculations with light, using silicon photonic circuits and metamaterial components.

TechFlow says the company recently closed a $110 million Series A round led by Gates Frontier, with Microsoft's investment arm M12, Carbon Direct Capital, Aramco Ventures, Bosch Ventures, Tectonic Ventures, Space Capital and others; the money lets it roughly quadruple its team in 2026.

Claim: because the optical core needs no on-chip switches, an OCU does roughly 25 times more operations per second than a GPU of the same chip size and power budget; elsewhere the article says about 50 times faster and 35 times more energy efficient for a full tensor core.
Neurophos says its metamaterial modulators are about 10,000 times smaller than state-of-the-art ones, so a million can fit on a fingernail-size chip.
Photonic memory does not yet exist, so the chip still depends on conventional memory (SRAM, DRAM) and on converting between light and electricity at its inputs and outputs.

The company has completed computational demonstrations of its first metasurface array and is preparing further devices; Microsoft is an investor and the company names partnerships with hyperscale cloud providers.
Yole Group, a market research firm, expects the first wave of OCUs to be deployed in 2028 and the market to reach about $2.7 billion by 2034.
CEO Patrick Bowen is quoted: Moore's Law is slowing but AI cannot wait, and photonics offers a way past the power limits of GPUs.
quote_evidence: Consequently, at the same chip size and power budget, an OCU completes roughly 25 times more operations per second than a GPU.
According to Yole Group, the first wave of OCUs is expected to deploy in 2028, with the market potentially expanding to around $2.7 billion by 2034 (roughly one million units).
The company has completed computational demonstrations of its first metasurface array and is tape-outing further devices focused on reliability and performance enhancements.
why_it_matters_hint: Chips that compute with light could cut the power AI data centres need, but the performance figures are the company's own and the product is not yet on sale.
event_date: 22 Jan 2026 (Series A announced; TechFlow's article is undated and says 'recently')
notes: OLDER NEWS RE-DATED: the $110 million Series A was announced about 22 Jan 2026 (SiliconANGLE, 22 Jan 2026; also reported by Data Center Dynamics, The Register and Optics.org in Jan 2026). TechFlow's 12 Oct 2026 article is an explainer that does not name its original author and does not date the round. Performance figures vary by source: 25x here, 50x and 35x later in the same article, up to 100x on SiliconANGLE; all are company claims. SiliconANGLE calls the product an optical processing unit (OPU), TechFlow an optical computing unit (OCU).
